questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has 3 hours of sudden, severe central abdominal pain. She is writhing and has vomited. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft with only mild central tenderness and no guarding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden severe pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen, in a patient with a valvular lesion (embolic source) and a raised lactate, is acute mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: soft with only mild central tenderness
steps.x: **Valvular disease** = embolic source. **Pain out of proportion** to a soft abdomen. Raised **lactate**.

elim: The amylase is normal.
RUQ pain without a raised lactate.
Would give a rigid abdomen early.
Loin-to-groin pain; no lactic acidosis.

steps.x: **A. Acute mesenteric ischaemia.** Severe pain + soft abdomen + embolic source + high lactate = acute mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has sudden severe central abdominal pain that began an hour ago. Shortly after, he had an urgent, forceful bowel movement containing dark blood. He has no previous bowel problems. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. His abdomen is soft. His ECG is shown; he has never had an abnormal heart rhythm before.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG on arrival
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden pain followed by forceful bowel evacuation that may contain blood, with new-onset AF as the embolic source, is mesenteric infarction from an SMA embolus.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: urgent, forceful bowel movement containing dark blood
never had an abnormal heart rhythm before
steps.x: **New-onset AF** + sudden pain + **gut emptying** with blood: the classic embolic picture.

elim: Painless, large-volume bleeding.
Bright red blood on the paper, with no severe pain.
Not sudden severe pain with a soft abdomen and new AF.
Unlikely new onset at 77 with sudden pain and a new arrhythmia.

steps.x: **D. Mesenteric infarction.** New AF + sudden pain + bowel evacuation with blood = mesenteric infarction.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and previous coronary stents has lost 9 kg in 5 months. She gets central abdominal pain about 20 minutes after eating that lasts an hour. She now eats very small amounts. Her OGD, colonoscopy and CT abdomen show no tumour.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for her weight loss?
o: Fear of eating because of post-prandial pain
questions.e: In chronic mesenteric ischaemia, post-prandial 'abdominal angina' makes patients afraid to eat (sitophobia), causing weight loss. She has a strong atherosclerotic background.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely reason for her weight loss? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Atherosclerosis + **pain after meals** + eating less: **food fear**.

elim: Malabsorption with diarrhoea; pain is not meal-timed in this way.
Does not cause pain after meals.
Weight loss despite a good appetite.
Excluded by endoscopy and CT.

steps.x: **C. Fear of eating because of post-prandial pain.** Chronic mesenteric ischaemia: weight loss from food fear (sitophobia).

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman had 2 days of profuse vomiting with a low BP from gastroenteritis. Today she has crampy left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Colonoscopy shows a segment of oedematous, ulcerated mucosa around the splenic flexure with a normal rectum. Stool cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Crampy left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea after hypoperfusion, affecting the watershed splenic flexure with rectal sparing, is ischaemic colitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: crampy left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea
splenic flexure with a normal rectum
steps.x: **Hypoperfusion**, then left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea at the **splenic flexure** watershed.

elim: Follows antibiotics; pseudomembranes and not segmental at the splenic flexure.
Unusual new onset at 78 after a hypotensive episode.
Painless, without ulcerated mucosa.
Starts in the rectum and spreads proximally; her rectum is normal.

steps.x: **D. Ischaemic colitis.** Bloody diarrhoea after hypotension, splenic flexure, rectal sparing = ischaemic colitis.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man was admitted 2 days ago with ischaemic colitis, with severe pain and frequent loose bloody stools. Today the stools have slowed, but his pain is diffuse and constant and his abdomen is distended and quiet. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. He is not yet shocked.
questions.q: Which phase of ischaemic colitis is he most likely to be in?
questions.e: Ischaemic colitis progresses from a hyperactive phase (severe pain, frequent bloody stools) to a paralytic phase (diffuse constant pain, distension, fewer stools) and then a shock phase.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which phase of ischaemic colitis is he most likely to be in? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fewer stools + **diffuse constant pain** + **distension**: the bowel has stopped moving.

elim: Severe pain with frequent bloody stools; this was his presentation.
Not a recognised phase.
His pain is worse and his abdomen is distended.
He is not yet shocked.

steps.x: **B. Paralytic phase.** Ischaemic colitis: hyperactive → paralytic → shock.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with factor V Leiden takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has had 4 days of gradually worsening, poorly localised abdominal pain with nausea. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her abdomen is mildly tender. She is in sinus rhythm. Contrast CT shows a filling defect in the superior mesenteric vein with bowel wall thickening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bowel ischaemia?
questions.e: Venous thrombosis is a cause of intestinal ischaemia, typically in hypercoagulable patients, with a more gradual onset. Venous outflow obstruction impairs perfusion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her bowel ischaemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Hypercoagulable** + **gradual** onset + clot in the **vein**.

elim: No systemic features, and the CT shows a venous clot.
She is not shocked.
Sudden onset, usually with AF; she is in sinus rhythm.
Occurs on atherosclerosis in older patients.

steps.x: **B. Mesenteric venous thrombosis.** Young, prothrombotic, gradual pain = mesenteric venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man in intensive care is on high-dose noradrenaline for septic shock from pneumonia. Over 12 hours he develops abdominal distension and his lactate rises to 7.2 mmol/L. He is in sinus rhythm. CT mesenteric angiography shows no vessel occlusion but diffuse narrowing of the mesenteric arcades.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bowel ischaemia?
questions.e: Systemic hypoperfusion (shock, vasopressors) is a cause of intestinal ischaemia; CT angiography shows vasoconstriction of the mesenteric arcades rather than a proximal occlusion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his bowel ischaemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Shock** + vasopressors + **no occlusion** + **narrowed arcades**.

elim: The CT shows no venous clot.
No occlusion is seen and he is in sinus rhythm.
No occlusion is seen.
A complication of colitis; the vessels would be normal.

steps.x: **B. Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia from hypoperfusion.** Ischaemia in shock without a clot = non-occlusive (hypoperfusion) ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man who smokes and has intermittent claudication has had 4 months of central abdominal pain after meals and has lost 7 kg. Today he has sudden, severe, constant central abdominal pain. He is in sinus rhythm. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 156/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His abdomen is soft. His lactate is 5.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acute pain?
questions.e: Months of post-prandial pain (chronic ischaemia from atherosclerosis), then sudden severe pain, is acute-on-chronic SMA thrombosis on a pre-existing stenosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his acute pain? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 4 months of central abdominal pain after meals
steps.x: **Atherosclerosis** with **abdominal angina** first, then acute pain, in **sinus rhythm**: the stenosis has thrombosed.

elim: Usually gradual onset in a hypercoagulable patient.
He is not shocked or on vasopressors.
He is hypertensive and not shocked, with no back pain.
He is in sinus rhythm with no embolic source, and there is a chronic history.

steps.x: **E. Superior mesenteric artery thrombosis.** Previous abdominal angina + sudden pain = SMA thrombosis; AF + sudden pain = SMA embolus.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with atrial fibrillation presented 14 hours ago with severe central abdominal pain and a soft abdomen. Theatre was delayed. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 134 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. She now winces when the bed is moved.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her abdomen now?
questions.e: Late in mesenteric ischaemia, transmural infarction causes peritonitis: guarding, rebound tenderness and shock.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her abdomen now? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: winces when the bed is moved
steps.x: Hours later, **shocked** and in pain with movement: the bowel has infarcted through its wall.

elim: Seen early; she has now progressed.
A sign of aortic aneurysm.
Cholecystitis.
Typical of appendicitis.

steps.x: **A. Guarding and rebound tenderness.** Late mesenteric ischaemia: guarding, peritonitis, shock.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped his apixaban a week ago has 2 hours of abdominal pain. He is in severe distress and has vomited. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. The surgical registrar is worried about mesenteric ischaemia.
questions.q: Which examination finding most supports this diagnosis?
o: Palpable tender mass in the right iliac fossa
Soft abdomen with minimal tenderness despite severe pain
questions.e: 'Pain out of proportion to examination findings' is the classic description of acute mesenteric ischaemia: severe pain with a soft, barely tender abdomen early on.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which examination finding most supports this diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**AF off anticoagulation** = embolic risk. Early ischaemia gives **pain without peritonism**.

elim: A sign of perforation or late infarction, not early ischaemia.
Suggests an appendix mass.
Appendicitis.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm.

steps.x: **E. Soft abdomen with minimal tenderness despite severe pain.** Acute mesenteric ischaemia = pain out of proportion to examination.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her warfarin 5 days ago before a planned procedure. She has 4 hours of sudden severe central abdominal pain and has vomited twice. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 146/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft and minimally tender. Her venous lactate is 5.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: AF with interrupted anticoagulation is a major risk for SMA embolus; sudden severe pain with a soft abdomen and raised lactate is acute mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**AF off warfarin**, **sudden** pain, **soft** abdomen, raised **lactate**.

elim: RUQ pain without lactic acidosis.
Would not give sudden severe pain with a high lactate.
Left iliac fossa pain with fever and localised tenderness.
Diarrhoea and vomiting, but not severe pain with a soft abdomen and high lactate.

steps.x: **A. Acute mesenteric ischaemia.** AF + sudden severe pain + soft abdomen + high lactate = acute mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes 30 a day has intermittent claudication and a previous myocardial infarction. For 6 months he has had dull central abdominal pain 15 to 30 minutes after meals and he has lost 10 kg. His OGD and colonoscopy are normal. His amylase and liver tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Post-prandial 'abdominal angina' with weight loss in a patient with widespread atherosclerosis is chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Atherosclerosis** everywhere + **pain after meals** + weight loss + normal scopes.

elim: Usually alcohol-related, with steatorrhoea; amylase and imaging may be abnormal.
RUQ pain after fatty meals with normal weight.
Excluded by a normal OGD.
Excluded by a normal OGD.

steps.x: **A. Chronic mesenteric ischaemia.** Abdominal angina + weight loss + vascular disease = chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman had an emergency laparotomy 3 months ago for acute mesenteric ischaemia, with resection of most of her small bowel; 80 cm remains. She now has watery diarrhoea 8 times a day, has lost 12 kg and has low magnesium and vitamin B12 levels despite eating well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Extensive small bowel resection after mesenteric infarction leaves too little absorptive surface: short bowel syndrome, with diarrhoea, weight loss and micronutrient deficiencies.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: resection of most of her small bowel
steps.x: Too little **small bowel** left after **extensive resection**.

elim: Does not explain the global malabsorption after massive resection.
Would not cause months of malabsorption with micronutrient deficiencies.
Unrelated to her surgery.
Would cause pain, not this pattern of malabsorption.

steps.x: **E. Short bowel syndrome.** Massive resection for mesenteric infarction → short bowel syndrome.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with atrial fibrillation has 3 hours of severe central abdominal pain with a soft abdomen. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, irregularly irregular, and BP 140/84 mmHg. He has vomited twice. His lactate is 4.9 mmol/L. He has CT mesenteric angiography.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his CT mesenteric angiogram?
o: Occlusion of the proximal superior mesenteric artery
questions.e: CT mesenteric angiography, the gold standard, shows proximal occlusion of the mesenteric vessels (often an SMA embolus in AF) or vasoconstriction of the arcades.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on his CT mesenteric angiogram? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
AF embolus lodges in the **SMA**; the angiogram shows the **occlusion**.

elim: A sign of perforation.
Cholecystitis.
Diverticulitis.
Pancreatitis.

steps.x: **C. Occlusion of the proximal superior mesenteric artery.** CT mesenteric angiography in AMI: proximal SMA occlusion.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has sudden severe abdominal pain, a soft abdomen and a lactate of 5.8 mmol/L. Mesenteric infarction is suspected. The radiologist asks how the CT should be performed to answer the question.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate CT protocol?
o: CT kidneys, ureters and bladder without contrast
questions.e: Suspected mesenteric infarction needs an arterial phase CT (CT mesenteric angiography), the gold standard, to show the vessels.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate CT protocol? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
To see an **occluded artery** you need contrast timed for the **arterial phase**.

elim: For colonic polyps and tumours, not ischaemia.
For renal stones.
For the urinary tract.
Cannot show the vessels.

steps.x: **A. Arterial phase CT angiography.** Suspected mesenteric ischaemia = arterial phase CT angiography.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man with atrial fibrillation has 4 hours of severe central abdominal pain. His abdomen is soft. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A venous blood gas is taken while CT is arranged.
questions.q: Which venous blood gas result is most likely?
o: pH 7.24, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, pCO2 3.9 kPa, lactate 6.1 mmol/L
pH 7.30, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, pCO2 8.2 kPa, lactate 1.0 mmol/L
pH 7.40, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, pCO2 5.3 kPa, lactate 1.1 mmol/L
pH 7.48, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, pCO2 3.6 kPa, lactate 1.2 mmol/L
pH 7.52, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, pCO2 5.9 kPa, lactate 1.4 mmol/L
questions.e: Ischaemic bowel causes a metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, HCO3 <22, pCO2 <4.7 kPa as compensation) with a raised lactate.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which venous blood gas result is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Ischaemia = **metabolic acidosis** with **raised lactate**; the fast breathing is compensation.

elim: Respiratory acidosis.
Normal.
Respiratory alkalosis.
Metabolic alkalosis, as in vomiting.

steps.x: **A. pH 7.24, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, pCO2 3.9 kPa, lactate 6.1 mmol/L.** AMI blood gas: low pH, low HCO3, low pCO2, high lactate.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is resuscitated while awaiting CT. She has atrial fibrillation and has been given IV fluids, heparin and antibiotics. Her pain is unchanged and her abdomen remains soft. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. Her lactate is measured repeatedly, as shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these results?
o: Expected lactate rise from IV fluids
questions.e: Lactate is a sensitive indicator of ongoing ischaemia from anaerobic metabolism; a rising lactate despite resuscitation means the bowel is still ischaemic and surgery is urgent.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for these results? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Rising **lactate** despite fluids = the bowel is still **ischaemic**.

elim: IV fluids do not cause a rising lactate.
A consistent rising trend is real.
Lactate would fall.
Causes alkalosis, not a rising lactate.

steps.x: **C. Ongoing bowel ischaemia.** Rising lactate in suspected AMI = ongoing ischaemia; escalate.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman who smokes has 8 months of central abdominal pain 30 minutes after meals and 9 kg weight loss. She has carotid and coronary artery disease. OGD and colonoscopy are normal. The vascular team suspect chronic mesenteric ischaemia and plan to treat it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: CT mesenteric angiography confirms mesenteric stenosis or occlusion and plans angioplasty; lactate is usually normal in chronic disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Abdominal angina + atherosclerosis: confirm the **stenosis** by imaging the **vessels**.

elim: Cannot show the vessels.
Looks at the small bowel mucosa, not the vessels.
Tests pancreatic exocrine function.
Usually normal in chronic ischaemia.

steps.x: **C. CT mesenteric angiography.** Mesenteric ischaemia (acute or chronic) is confirmed by CT mesenteric angiography.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with atrial fibrillation has 5 hours of severe abdominal pain and a soft abdomen. His respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96%. He has an arterial blood gas while breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of this blood gas?
questions.e: Low pH with low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis; the low pCO2 is respiratory compensation. The raised lactate from ischaemic bowel is the cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely interpretation of this blood gas? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: severe abdominal pain and a soft abdomen
steps.x: pH **low**, HCO3 **low** = metabolic acidosis. pCO2 **low** = breathing it off. Lactate **high**.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are low, not high.
The pH is low.
pH, bicarbonate and lactate are abnormal.
The pCO2 is low, not high.

steps.x: **A. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.** AMI: lactic metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia. CT angiography is booked. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft. Her lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Discharge with oral analgesia and outpatient CT
Encourage oral intake and give laxatives
Nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, IV heparin and urgent surgical review
questions.e: First-line management is ABCDE, urgent surgical review, nil by mouth, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and IV heparin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Resuscitate, stop the clot extending (**heparin**), cover translocating bacteria (**antibiotics**), call the **surgeons**.

elim: A life-threatening emergency.
She must be nil by mouth.
Inadequate; she needs IV heparin and surgical review.
Not the investigation or treatment for AMI.

steps.x: **C. Nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, IV heparin and urgent surgical review.** AMI first-line: NBM, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, IV heparin, urgent surgical review.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with atrial fibrillation has had 2 hours of severe central abdominal pain. CT angiography shows an embolus in the proximal superior mesenteric artery with normal-appearing bowel and no free fluid. His abdomen is soft with no guarding. He has been given IV heparin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Embolectomy can restore flow if necrosis has not yet occurred. If there is peritonitis or non-viable bowel, laparotomy and resection are needed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Early**, **embolus**, bowel still **viable**: remove the clot.

elim: An operation for sigmoid perforation.
The occlusion must be relieved before the bowel dies.
Treats chronic stenosis, not an acute embolus.
Not indicated; the bowel is still viable.

steps.x: **A. Embolectomy.** Embolus with viable bowel = embolectomy; necrotic bowel = laparotomy and resection.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has an emergency laparotomy for acute mesenteric ischaemia. A 1 metre segment of black, non-viable small bowel is resected. The remaining bowel looks dusky but may recover. The ends are left stapled and the abdomen is temporarily closed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start an oral diet the next day
questions.e: After resection of non-viable bowel, a second 'relook' laparotomy is often done the next day to check the viability of the remaining bowel.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Some bowel is **doubtful**: take another look before deciding to join it.

elim: Not relevant to the viability of the small bowel.
She has just had a damage-control laparotomy.
Treats chronic stenosis; does not assess bowel viability.
She needs a relook before the bowel is joined.

steps.x: **D. Relook laparotomy within 24 to 48 hours.** AMI laparotomy: resect dead bowel, then relook laparotomy the next day.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with chronic mesenteric ischaemia has a tight superior mesenteric artery stenosis successfully treated with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and stenting. He smokes 20 a day and has hypertension and a raised LDL cholesterol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
questions.e: The definitive treatment for chronic mesenteric ischaemia is angioplasty plus risk factor modification: stop smoking, antiplatelet and statin, blood pressure control.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The artery is open; now treat the **atherosclerosis** that caused it.

elim: Not a long-term treatment.
Does not address atherosclerosis.
Not indicated; the bowel is viable.
Not indicated and harmful to the gut.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation, antiplatelet and statin.** Chronic mesenteric ischaemia: angioplasty + risk factor modification.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has ischaemic colitis after a hypotensive episode. Despite IV fluids and antibiotics, after 2 days she has worsening pain, a rigid tender abdomen and rising lactate. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. CT shows a thin-walled, non-enhancing descending colon with free fluid.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue supportive care for another 48 hours
questions.e: Ischaemic colitis is usually managed with supportive care and antibiotics; surgery (resection of the dead colon) is reserved for severe cases with peritonitis, gangrene or shock.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Supportive care has **failed**: peritonitis, shock and **non-enhancing** (dead) colon.

elim: She is deteriorating with signs of gangrene.
Treats ulcerative colitis, not ischaemia.
Not the treatment for gangrenous colitis.
Risky and does not treat the problem.

steps.x: **B. Emergency colectomy.** Ischaemic colitis: supportive care + antibiotics; surgery only for severe disease.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with atrial fibrillation has 10 hours of abdominal pain. He now has guarding and rebound tenderness. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. CT angiography shows an occluded superior mesenteric artery with gas in the small bowel wall. He has had IV fluids, heparin and antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Embolectomy alone without inspecting the bowel
Emergency laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel
questions.e: With peritonitis, sepsis and signs of bowel necrosis, AMI needs immediate laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel; untreated necrosis leads to perforation and sepsis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: gas in the small bowel wall
steps.x: **Peritonitis** + **sepsis** + gas in the wall = **necrosis**.

elim: The bowel is likely necrotic and must be assessed and resected.
Not enough with peritonitis and necrosis.
For chronic stenosis.
Not appropriate with infarcted bowel and peritonitis.

steps.x: **B. Emergency laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel.** AMI with peritonitis or necrosis = emergency laparotomy and resection.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has 2 hours of agonising central abdominal pain. She needs IV morphine. Her abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, with no guarding. A student asks why the examination is so unremarkable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Morphine has masked the peritoneal signs
She has a high pain threshold
The ischaemia is visceral and has not yet reached the parietal peritoneum
The pain is referred from the heart
questions.e: Early pain is visceral ischaemic pain; peritoneal signs develop only once transmural infarction and peritonitis set in.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Severe **visceral** pain, but the **parietal peritoneum** is not yet involved.

elim: The pain was out of proportion before morphine; analgesia does not mask peritonitis.
Not a mechanism.
A dangerous assumption in AMI.
No cardiac features.

steps.x: **C. The ischaemia is visceral and has not yet reached the parietal peritoneum.** Pain out of proportion = visceral ischaemia before transmural infarction.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man develops ischaemic colitis after a long episode of hypotension during sepsis. He has crampy left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Colonoscopy shows patchy ischaemic mucosa at the splenic flexure and in a second region.
questions.q: Which other region of the colon is most vulnerable?
questions.e: Watershed areas, the splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction, receive blood from the most distal branches of two arterial territories and are most vulnerable to hypoperfusion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which other region of the colon is most vulnerable? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: splenic flexure and in a second region
steps.x: **Watershed** areas: the **splenic flexure** (SMA/IMA) and the **rectosigmoid junction**.

elim: Supplied centrally by the SMA (right colic).
Not a classic watershed area.
Supplied by the SMA (right and middle colic).
Supplied centrally by the middle colic artery.

steps.x: **D. Rectosigmoid junction.** Watershed = splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with a 70% superior mesenteric artery stenosis has no pain when fasting, but central abdominal pain starts 20 to 30 minutes after a large meal and lasts 2 hours. She has lost 6 kg and smokes. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pain?
o: Blood flow cannot rise to meet the increased metabolic demand of digestion
Gastric distension causing visceral stretch pain
Sudden embolic occlusion after each meal
questions.e: Ischaemia occurs when blood flow cannot meet metabolic demand. Digestion increases gut demand; a fixed stenosis prevents the rise in flow, causing 'abdominal angina'.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has 2 days of crampy left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea after a hypotensive episode. Her abdominal X-ray shows thickened bowel wall with rounded, finger-like indentations along the splenic flexure. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of this X-ray sign?
questions.e: 'Thumbprinting' in ischaemic colitis is caused by bowel wall (submucosal) oedema and haemorrhage indenting the lumen.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of this X-ray sign? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Thumbprinting** = the swollen, **oedematous** wall pushing into the lumen.

elim: Gives mottled faeces, not mural indentations.
A sign of perforation.
Causes gallstone ileus in the small bowel.
Seen in chronic ulcerative colitis.

steps.x: **A. Bowel wall oedema and haemorrhage.** Thumbprinting on AXR = bowel wall oedema in ischaemic colitis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a successful SMA embolectomy for acute mesenteric ischaemia after 6 hours of symptoms. Over the next few hours, the reperfused bowel becomes swollen, his potassium and lactate rise, and he becomes more unwell.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Fresh embolus to the same artery
questions.e: Restoring flow to ischaemic bowel causes reperfusion injury: free radicals, oedema, and release of potassium and lactate, which can progress to transmural infarction and perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Flow back to **ischaemic** tissue: oxygen free radicals, swelling, and release of **potassium** and **lactate** from anaerobic cells.

elim: Would cause hypotension with rash and wheeze, not bowel swelling.
Possible, but the reperfused bowel swelling points to reperfusion.
Does not cause bowel swelling and rising potassium.
Causes low potassium and phosphate after feeding.

steps.x: **E. Reperfusion injury.** After revascularisation, think reperfusion injury.
